name: Jenkins et al. (2003), national-scale estimators; open-grown trees at 0.8
source: Jenkins, J. C., Chojnacky, D. C., Heath, L. S. and Birdsey, R. A. (2003), National-scale biomass estimators for United States tree species, Forest Science 49: 12-35 (a work of the United States Government, in the public domain): above-ground dry biomass bm = exp(b0 + b1 ln dbh), kg, dbh in cm, for trees of 2.5 cm and more (Table 4); coarse roots as a ratio exp(b0 + b1/dbh) of it (Table 6); genera and species assigned to groups as Tables 1 and 3 assign them. Nowak, D. J. (1994), Atmospheric carbon dioxide reduction by Chicago's urban forest, in Chicago's Urban Forest Ecosystem, USDA Forest Service Gen. Tech. Rep. NE-186, pp. 83-94: open-grown urban trees at 0.8 of forest-grown biomass. Carbon as half the dry biomass.
notes: Jenkins et al. fitted their equations to North American forest trees. Genera they do not assign (Eucalyptus, Corymbia, Lophostemon, Allocasuarina and most of a southern city's trees) fall to the fallback group, and every estimate says that it did.

Ours, not Jenkins et al.'s: the families Pinaceae (to Pine) and Cupressaceae (to Cedar/larch), from the softwood genera their Table 3 assigns; the woodland group taking the hardwood ratio of roots (Table 6 gives hardwood and softwood only); the fallback, Mixed hardwood.

Residuals of single trees lie between -35% and +36% of the prediction (10th and 90th percentiles, their Table 5); totals over many trees are better than any one. No increments, heights or crowns are stated: the tools take increments from the inventory or as declared.
